overview: Steel & Tube Holdings is a New Zealand steel solutions company that sources, processes and distributes a broad range of steel, stainless, aluminium and metal products (fasteners, fire pipe & fittings, rural products, chain & rigging, roofing, structural coil, and reinforcing/mesh) through a nationwide network of roughly 35+ sites to over 13,000 active customers. In FY2025 it added galvanizing and metal-protection services via the Perry Metal Protection acquisition, and in FY2026 it announced the exit of its structurally challenged reinforcing/wire and plate-processing businesses. It is a small, cyclical, price-taking distributor whose fortunes track the depth of the New Zealand construction and manufacturing cycle, currently trading near multi-year-low prices after three consecutive loss-making years.

business_model.summary: Steel & Tube earns a product/gross margin per tonne on steel and metal products it buys from NZ Steel and offshore mills, holds as inventory, and either sells as-is (Distribution) or processes into higher-value formats (roofing/coil, purlins, ComFlor decking, reinforcing/mesh, and now hot-dip galvanizing and grating/sandblasting via Perry Metal Protection) before selling on a contract/project basis, sometimes including onsite installation. Margin is a function of volume (tonnes sold), product margin percentage (spread between input steel cost and selling price) and fixed operating cost absorption (operating leverage) rather than any structural pricing power. The business is working-capital intensive: inventory was ~$113.6m at FY25 year-end (~$115.9m at 1H26) and is directly exposed to global steel price swings — falling steel prices produce inventory holding losses that compress margins (as seen in FY2025 when product margin fell to 28.1% from 29.8%), while rising prices can produce holding gains. Revenue is transactional/project-based, not recurring or subscription-like, and is granular across a large customer base (no single customer dominates), though volumes are highly sensitive to the construction and manufacturing cycle.

revenue_streams.name: Distribution (Carbon Products, Stainless, Aluminium, Fire Pipe & Fittings, Rural, Fasteners, Chain & Rigging)
revenue_streams.trend: declining (cyclical trough, though improving into FY26)

revenue_streams.name: Processing (Roofing/Coil/Purlins/ComFlor/Reinforcing/Mesh/Galvanizing/Grating/Sandblasting)
revenue_streams.trend: mixed - core reinforcing/plate being exited FY26/27, galvanizing (Perry) growing

business_model.customer_type: B2B - trade, manufacturing, construction contractors and project customers; ~13,000 active customers, no material single-customer concentration disclosed
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand - nationwide network of ~35 sites from Whangarei to Invercargill; no meaningful international revenue
business_model.segment_end_markets_1H26: Manufacturing 39% of revenue, Non-Residential/Commercial construction 27%, Residential construction 19%, Agriculture & other 11%, Infrastructure 4%

main_competitors: Fletcher Building's Fletcher Steel stable (EasySteel, Fletcher Reinforcing, CSP Pacific, Fletcher Wire Products, Dimond Roofing, Dimond Structural, Pacific Coilcoaters)
Direct imports from China and other Asian mills (via importers and large contractors bypassing local distributors)
Various smaller regional fabricators and processors
competitive_position.market_position: One of the two or three largest full-range steel distributor/processors in New Zealand, but a clear second tier behind Fletcher Building's vertically integrated steel businesses in scale and balance-sheet strength; a price-taking participant in a commodity-like, fragmented market rather than a share leader with pricing power.

moat_factors.factor: National distribution network / breadth of range
moat_factors.description: Nationwide site network and New Zealand's most comprehensive steel product range support a one-stop-shop / cross-sell proposition and switching costs for smaller trade customers, but this is a scale advantage, not a structural barrier - a well-capitalised competitor (Fletcher, Vulcan) can replicate it.
High customer NPS (42 vs industry average 32 in FY25) and long-standing relationships support retention, but steel distribution remains price-sensitive and tender-driven, limiting pricing power.

Galvanizing has higher barriers to entry (capital-intensive plant, environmental permitting) than commodity distribution and management says Perry is performing ahead of business case, providing some earnings resilience through the cycle.

Long-established NZ brand (60+ years) but has been damaged by a history of profit warnings, impairments and a 2018 covenant breach/capital raise; brand alone does not command a price premium in a commodity product.

weaknesses: Fundamentally a low-differentiation, capital/working-capital-intensive commodity distributor with limited genuine pricing power - product margin is set by competitive tender activity and input steel costs, not brand or switching costs
No structural moat against import competition; large projects and sophisticated buyers can and do source directly from Asian mills when the NZD/steel price spread makes it worthwhile
Scale disadvantage versus Fletcher Building, which is vertically integrated (NZ Steel supply relationships, larger balance sheet, broader building-materials distribution via PlaceMakers/Winstone)

Reinforcing/wire and plate processing businesses being exited in FY26/27 were explicitly described by management as 'structurally challenged due to low barriers to entry' - an admission that parts of the portfolio never had a moat
Highly fragmented industry with excess supply capacity, which management itself cited as pressuring reinforcing/mesh pricing in FY2025
Balance sheet materially weaker than larger peers (net debt vs net cash historically), constraining ability to invest counter-cyclically or withstand a prolonged downturn

growth_drivers: NZ construction and infrastructure recovery: MBIE National Construction Pipeline forecasts a gradual rise to $65.4bn by 2030; management points to improving PMI and building consents and a NZ$181bn national infrastructure pipeline (per NZ Infrastructure Commission, Sept 2025) as tailwinds, though timing has repeatedly disappointed

Falling interest rates improving housing affordability and mortgage refinancing (roughly half of fixed-rate mortgages due for renewal within six months as of the FY25 report), expected to lift residential and eventually commercial construction demand
Government-backed infrastructure and social housing spend flagged for the second half of calendar 2026 - a repeated management talking point that has yet to materially show up in reported volumes

Mix-shift toward higher-value processing and services - galvanizing (Perry Metal Protection), grating and sandblasting, aluminium range expansion (aluminium sales +20% YoY in FY25), Kiwi Pipe & Fittings expansion into the South Island, new QBT450 roofing profile

Three successive annualised cost-out programmes (~$5m FY24, ~$7m FY25, further cost actions in FY26) that create operating leverage - a normalising economy should flow disproportionately to EBITDA given the now-smaller, more variable fixed cost base

Portfolio simplification: exiting reinforcing/wire (Euro Corporation deal, pending Commerce Commission approval) and plate processing and consolidating seven smaller sites is expected to remove a combined ~$7.5m of normalised EBIT losses and generate ~$11-12m of proceeds plus a ~$2m net cash benefit by FY27, freeing capital and management focus for the remaining higher-return businesses
Agriculture and rural sector has been a relative bright spot supporting volumes when construction has been weak, providing some diversification

business.risk: Depth and duration of the NZ construction downturn
business.description: Management has now described three consecutive 'most challenging' years; FY2025 volumes fell 12% YoY and revenue fell 20% to $385.4m; recovery has been repeatedly pushed out (FY25 outlook expected easing by 'early 2026,' which did not materialize into profitability, and FY26 result still showed a loss with management now guiding to only a 'gradual and uneven' recovery into calendar 2027).

business.risk: Steel price volatility and inventory holding losses
business.description: With inventory around $114-116m, falling global/import steel prices compress product margin and can trigger inventory write-downs; margin dropped from 29.8% (FY24) to 28.1% (FY25) partly on pricing pressure, before recovering to 31.1% in 1H26.

Direct imports from China and other Asian mills compete with local distribution/processing, particularly on large projects and commodity products, capping pricing power; NZ anti-dumping duties on some steel categories partially offset this but coverage is incomplete and subject to periodic review.

Management itself concluded reinforcing/wire and plate processing were structurally challenged with low barriers to entry, and is exiting them - evidence that parts of the historical business model lacked a genuine moat.
Large project wins are lumpy; loss of a few large contracts or project delays (e.g., Government infrastructure timing) has an outsized effect on a business of this size.

financial.risk: Leveraged balance sheet after the Perry Metal Protection acquisition
financial.description: Net position swung from net cash of $17.5m (1H25) to net debt of $43.0m (1H26) and ~$48m at FY26 year-end, funding the debt-financed acquisition and ongoing operating losses; this occurred while the company was posting consecutive statutory losses (NLAT -$24.4m FY25, -$61.2m FY26 including impairment), a combination that materially raises financial risk for a company of this size.

ANZ facilities were renewed/extended to September 2027 with revised covenants following the FY26 result - a sign the prior facility needed renegotiation given deteriorating credit metrics; further earnings disappointment could pressure covenant headroom again.

financial.risk: Large non-cash impairments signal impaired capital returns
financial.description: FY26 booked a $51.9m impairment of business-unit carrying values plus $3.8m other non-trading adjustments - the second major impairment episode in the company's history (after 2018) - highlighting that significant shareholder capital deployed into acquired/organic businesses has not earned an adequate return.

Market capitalisation of roughly NZ$50m (at ~NZ$0.305/share) and thin daily trading volumes mean the stock can be volatile on small trades and difficult to exit in size; wide bid-ask spreads are typical of NZX micro-caps.
No dividend has been declared since the downturn deepened; capital is being directed to debt reduction, removing the income support that previously underpinned the stock for yield-seeking holders.

regulatory.risk: Commerce Commission approval risk on reinforcing/wire divestment
regulatory.description: The Euro Corporation deal for the reinforcing/wire assets requires Commerce Commission clearance; delay or blocked approval would slow the promised balance-sheet repair and cash realisation.

Climate reporting entity status and net-zero commitments (118 kgCO2e/tonne sold disclosed FY25) could add compliance costs, particularly around the galvanizing operations which involve chemical processes.

macro.risk: NZ interest rate and mortgage-refinancing cycle
macro.description: Residential and commercial construction demand is highly sensitive to the OCR and fixed mortgage rate resets; the bull case depends on rate cuts translating into consent and construction activity, a transmission that has been slower than management has repeatedly forecast.

Both the FY25 and FY26 outlook statements rely on Government-backed infrastructure and social housing projects materialising 'in the latter half of calendar 2026' or into 2027; this has already been pushed out multiple times and is a political/fiscal decision outside the company's control.

macro.risk: General NZ economic cycle / recession sensitivity
macro.description: Revenue is heavily levered to manufacturing (39% of 1H26 revenue) and construction (50% combined residential/non-residential), both highly cyclical and currently in one of the deepest downturns since the early 1990s per management's own characterisation.

Product costs are influenced by global steel prices (often USD- or export-parity-linked) and NZD exchange rates; currency weakness raises input costs and can compress margin if not fully passed through.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ construction sector activity is forecast by MBIE's National Construction Pipeline Report to recover gradually and grow to roughly NZ$65.4bn by 2030, but the near-term trajectory has been repeatedly pushed back; management now characterises the recovery as 'gradual and uneven rather than a sharp rebound,' with meaningful improvement not expected until calendar 2027.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - Steel & Tube is a textbook late-early-cycle industrial distributor; volumes and margins move directly with construction consents, non-residential build activity, manufacturing PMI and infrastructure spending, with a multi-year trough evident from FY2022 (volume 167kt) through FY2025 (101.7kt) and only partial recovery through 1H26 (annualised ~108kt pace).
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - falling OCR and mortgage rates are explicitly cited by management as the primary transmission mechanism for demand recovery via housing affordability, consents and business investment confidence; the company itself carries net debt so higher-for-longer rates also raise its own funding costs.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: Moderate - steel products are sourced from both NZ Steel and offshore (largely Asian) mills; a weaker NZD raises landed input costs, which the company must pass through via product margin, but no hedging or FX detail is disclosed at a granular level.

recent_developments.event: FY2025 (year to 30 June 2025) results: revenue $385.4m (down 20% YoY), volumes 101.7kt (down 12%), product margin 28.1% (FY24: 29.8%), normalised EBITDA $2.1m (positive but down sharply from $35.8m FY24), statutory NLAT -$24.4m including $(4.6)m non-trading adjustments; net debt $36.3m including $30m for the Perry Metal Protection acquisition; no dividend declared; ~$7m annualised cost-out delivered.

Perry Metal Protection (galvanizing) integration continued; management reported the acquisition exceeded year-1 normalised EBIT-before-corporate-levy target within the first 8 months of ownership and integration/cross-selling synergies were on track.

Six months to 31 December 2025: revenue $211.9m (+8.1% YoY), volumes 54,213t (+11.3% YoY from 48,667t), product margin improved to 31.1% (1H25: 28.7%/27.5% depending on measure), normalised EBITDA $2.8m (1H25: $2.0m), but statutory NLAT -$12.4m (1H25: -$10.4m) and normalised EBIT still -$10.3m; net debt swung to $43.0m from net cash $17.5m a year earlier, driven by the debt-funded galvanizing acquisition and ongoing operating losses; no dividend; management framed the result as 'primed for upside as the cycle turns.'

'Renewed Bank Facilities & Trading Update' NZX announcement - company renegotiated/extended its ANZ banking facilities ahead of full-year results, consistent with balance-sheet strain from consecutive losses and rising net debt.

FY2026 (year to 30 June 2026) results: revenue up 13.9% YoY, volumes up 15.9% YoY - clear recovery in trading activity after three recessionary years; normalised EBITDA surged to $9.9m from $2.1m (+376%) and normalised EBIT improved 23.7%, with 2H26 earnings ~40% better than 1H26. However, the company booked a $51.9m impairment of business-unit carrying values plus $3.8m of other non-trading adjustments, producing a statutory loss after tax of $61.2m - by far the company's largest loss since the 2018 crisis. Net debt was approximately $48m, broadly stable through the second half. ANZ banking facilities were extended to September 2027 with revised covenants. Dividends remain on hold and M&A is paused while the company prioritises debt reduction.

Strategic reset: Steel & Tube announced it is exiting its reinforcing and wire business (which lost an estimated $7.5m in normalised EBIT in FY26 and was described by management as 'structurally challenged due to low barriers to entry') via an agreement with Euro Corporation, subject to Commerce Commission approval, plus exiting plate processing and consolidating seven smaller sites. Expected to generate NZ$11-12m in proceeds from asset/inventory sales and a ~$2m net cash benefit by end of FY27.

CEO Mark Malpass declined to give formal FY27 guidance, stating the recovery would be 'gradual and uneven rather than a sharp rebound,' with 1H FY27 likely to remain variable and manufacturing/rural sectors expected to be more resilient than commercial construction; stronger momentum is now pushed out to calendar year 2027.

Market reaction to FY26 results was negative given the size of the statutory loss and impairment despite improving underlying trading metrics; analyst price targets and sentiment reportedly softened following the release, though liquidity is thin and price quotes vary by source.

items.notes: Management explicitly declined to give formal quantitative guidance, citing macro uncertainty; described recovery as 'gradual and uneven' with 1H FY27 likely to remain variable.

items.metric: Cash proceeds from reinforcing/wire and site divestments
items.notes: Expected from asset and inventory sales tied to exit of reinforcing/wire, plate processing and consolidation of seven smaller sites; Euro Corporation deal for reinforcing/wire pending Commerce Commission approval.

items.metric: Net cash benefit from site consolidation
items.notes: From consolidating seven smaller sites as part of the portfolio simplification.
Capital prioritised toward debt reduction and balance-sheet repair; no near-term resumption signalled.

items.vs_prior: lowered (from active M&A pipeline in FY24/25)
items.notes: Explicit reversal of the prior 'fast-track scale through M&A' strategy following the debt-funded Perry Metal Protection acquisition.

items.target: ANZ facilities extended with revised covenants
items.notes: Management described the renewal as providing 'financial stability and flexibility,' but the need for revised covenants after successive losses is itself a signal of prior covenant/headroom pressure.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Mark Malpass: recovery will be 'gradual and uneven rather than a sharp rebound,' with manufacturing and rural sectors expected to remain more resilient than commercial construction, and stronger momentum not expected until calendar year 2027. Management called the FY26 statutory loss 'disappointing' despite improved underlying trading (normalised EBITDA +376% YoY to $9.9m), and stated the immediate focus is 'restoring the strength of the balance sheet and returning the business to sustainable profitability' rather than growth. The $51.9m impairment was characterised as non-cash and potentially reversible if performance improves, but represents a formal write-down of the value the board itself had previously carried certain business units at.

bull_case: Underlying trading is genuinely recovering, not just improving off zero: FY26 volumes +15.9% and revenue +13.9% YoY, with normalised EBITDA up nearly 5x to $9.9m and 2H26 earnings ~40% ahead of 1H26 - the operating business appears to have bottomed and cost-out programmes are now showing clear operating leverage as volumes return

Portfolio simplification (exiting reinforcing/wire and plate processing, admitted by management to lack durable moats) should remove a combined ~$7.5m of normalised EBIT drag and free ~$11-12m of cash plus management attention to focus on higher-return Distribution and galvanizing/value-add businesses
Perry Metal Protection (galvanizing) is performing ahead of its acquisition business case and adds a more defensible, higher-margin, less commodity-like earnings stream than legacy steel distribution

Multiple concurrent NZ macro tailwinds - falling OCR/mortgage rates, improving PMI and building consents, and a large ($181bn) long-dated national infrastructure pipeline - provide several independent catalysts for demand recovery even if timing of any one is uncertain

Valuation is depressed and pricing in continued distress: trading well below net tangible assets at a ~NZ$50m market cap with a beaten-down share price near multi-year lows, offering asymmetric upside if the cycle inflects and the simplified, deleveraged business returns to the double-digit normalised EBITDA it earned at mid-cycle volumes in FY2021-23
bear_case: This is the third loss-making year in a row and the second major impairment/balance-sheet-repair episode in the company's history (2018 and now 2026), suggesting a structurally challenged, low-moat commodity distribution business rather than a temporary cyclical dip - management's own admission that reinforcing/wire had 'low barriers to entry' could equally apply to large parts of the remaining Distribution business

The balance sheet swung from net cash to ~$48m net debt at FY26 year-end to fund a debt-financed acquisition made in the depths of a downturn, precisely when leverage is most dangerous; ANZ's revised covenants after the FY26 loss signal the bank required renegotiated terms, and a further downturn or slower-than-hoped recovery could reopen covenant risk

Management's own 'primed for upside as the cycle turns' framing has now been used across at least two consecutive results (1H26 and FY25 outlook) while the recovery has repeatedly been pushed further out - the FY25 report expected easing by 'early 2026'; by August 2026 management was pushing meaningful improvement out to calendar 2027, a pattern of optimistic framing not yet matched by bottom-line results

No genuine moat: steel distribution margin is set by competitive tender activity, import competition from Asian mills, and global steel price movements, none of which the company controls; Fletcher Building's vertically integrated, larger-scale Fletcher Steel stable (EasySteel, Fletcher Reinforcing, Dimond) is a structurally stronger competitor with a bigger balance sheet

Small-cap illiquidity, suspended dividend, and a large, mostly non-cash impairment mean the stock offers no current income and depends entirely on a successful, and so far unproven, multi-year execution of both the portfolio exit programme and a genuine NZ construction upcycle materialising on the timeline management is now guiding to
